discovery: Quantum key distribution: founding quantum cryptography, including the BB84 protocol and entanglement-based key distribution

nominees.name: Charles H. Bennett
nominees.affiliation: IBM Thomas J. Watson Research Center, Yorktown Heights, USA

nominees.name: Artur Ekert
nominees.affiliation: University of Oxford, UK, and Centre for Quantum Technologies, National University of Singapore

motivation: Bennett and Brassard (BB84) showed that the quantum no-cloning principle and the disturbance caused by measurement make it possible to distribute secret keys whose security rests on the laws of physics, not on computational assumptions. Ekert (1991) linked this security directly to entanglement and the violation of Bell's inequality, so that a foundational test became a working cryptographic resource. Together these ideas created the field of quantum information, gave rise to quantum teleportation and device-independent security, and opened a global experimental programme that now includes fibre networks of hundreds of kilometres and satellite links between continents. Their work is a clear example of curiosity-driven research on the foundations of quantum mechanics turning into a new technology. It changed how physicists understand information itself, and it shaped a generation of experiments, including those recognised in 2022, which were in large part inspired by it.
